To fix Marginal Significance

What we found

You described 1 effect with terms related to ‘marginally significant’.

Show details

You described effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’. If p values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a p value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result.

Text Section Header
Consequently, frequentist approaches may yield significant effects, even when the strength of underlying evidence is minimal or uncertain (Moran & Linden, 2024). The present study

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate at which non-significant p-values are interpreted as marginally significant, see:

Olsson-Collentine A, van Assen MALM, Hartgerink CHJ (2019). “The Prevalence of Marginally Significant Results in Psychology Over Time.” Psychological Science, 30, 576–586. doi:10.1177/0956797619830326.

For the list of terms used to identifify marginally significant results, see this blog post by Matthew Hankins.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 30 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (30). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 6 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name install.packages() calls found
install_packages.R install.packages(missing_packages, dependencies = TRUE)

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 2 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 33 distinct packages/libraries: BayesFactor, bayestestR, BayesTools, brms, dplyr, esc, flextable, forcats, gemtc, ggplot2, ggridges, glue, grDevices, gridExtra, kableExtra, knitr, metafor, officer, patchwork, purrr, ragg, readr, readxl, rmarkdown, RoBMA, stats, stringr, tibble, tidybayes, tidyr, tidyverse, utils, viridis. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 133 files: 86 data, 29 code, 15 documentation, 3 materials.
  • We found 86 tabular data files and extracted 819 columns from 19 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 35 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy.
  • 1 file read as a table but is not a usable rectangular dataset (Included_articles_references_DOI.xlsx: 100% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: Included_articles_references_DOI.xlsx. We ran automated data-quality checks on 819 columns; 79 columns have at least one potential issue (40 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 19 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 11 columns with inconsistent category casing; 10 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 2 columns whose values look like personal information; 2 columns with leading/trailing whitespace). We detected demographic column for Age. 3 of 3 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 819 columns across 19 data files.

Issues Identified

85 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 19 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • fit_sensitivity_priors.R: “‘NoBMA’ is not an exported object from ‘namespace:RoBMA’”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

setwd() in the code

6 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

> latest_rds <- function(pattern, dir) {
>   files <- list.files(dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
>   files <- files[grepl("\\.rds$", files)]
>   if (!length(files)) return(NULL)
> 
>   # Handles both "2026-09-15 12:03:40.325364" and "20260915_120340" stamps.
>   stamp_key <- function(f) {
>     m <- regmatches(
>       f,
>       regexpr("[0-9]{4}-?[0-9]{2}-?[0-9]{2}[ _][0-9]{2}:?[0-9]{2}:?[0-9]{2}(\\.[0-9]+)?", f)
>     )
>     if (!length(m)) return(NA_character_)
>     d <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", m)               # digits only: lexical == chronological
>     substr(paste0(d, strrep("0", 20)), 1, 20)  # right-pad so widths are comparable
>   }
> 
>   key <- vapply(files, stamp_key, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
>   if (all(is.na(key))) return(files[which.max(file.info(files)$mtime)])
>   key[is.na(key)] <- ""
>   files[order(key, decreasing = TRUE)][1]
> }
> need_rds <- function(pattern, dir, what) {
>   f <- latest_rds(pattern, dir)
>   if (is.null(f)) stop("No .rds matching '", pattern, "' in ", dir,
>                        " (", what, "). Run run_analysis.R / fit_sensitivity_priors.R first.",
>                        call. = FALSE)
>   readRDS(f)
> }

> latest_rds <- function(pattern, dir = savD) {
>   files <- list.files(dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
>   files <- files[grepl("\\.rds$", files)]
>   if (length(files) == 0) return(NULL)
> 
>   # Handles both "2026-07-13 16:00:10.968897" and "20260730_123039" stamps.
>   stamp_key <- function(f) {
>     m <- regmatches(
>       f,
>       regexpr("[0-9]{4}-?[0-9]{2}-?[0-9]{2}[ _][0-9]{2}:?[0-9]{2}:?[0-9]{2}(\\.[0-9]+)?", f)
>     )
>     if (!length(m)) return(NA_character_)
>     d <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", m)                 # digits only: lexical == chronological
>     substr(paste0(d, strrep("0", 20)), 1, 20)  # right-pad so widths are comparable
>   }
> 
>   key <- vapply(files, stamp_key, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
>   if (all(is.na(key))) return(files[which.max(file.info(files)$mtime)])
>   key[is.na(key)] <- ""
>   files[order(key, decreasing = TRUE)][1]
> }
> nice_label <- function(x) gsub("_", " ", x)
> rename_outcome <- function(x) {
>   x <- as.character(x)
>   x <- gsub("Selective Attention\\s*/\\s*Inhibition\\s*\\(SAI\\)",
>             "Attentional Control (AC)", x)
>   x <- gsub("Selective Attention\\s*/\\s*Inhibition", "Attentional Control (AC)", x)
>   x
> }
> summary_rows <- list()
> flag_vec <- function(rhat, ess) {
>   ifelse(is.finite(rhat) & rhat > RHAT_BAD, "BAD",
>   ifelse((is.finite(rhat) & rhat > RHAT_WARN) |
>          (is.finite(ess)  & ess  < ESS_WARN), "WARN", "ok"))
> }
> diag_table <- function(fit) {
>   d <- tryCatch(summary(fit, type = "diagnostics"), error = function(e) NULL)
>   if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
> 
>   # --- Parameter-level (preferred) ---
>   est <- d$estimates
>   if (!is.null(est)) {
>     est <- as.data.frame(est)
>     if (nrow(est) > 0 && all(c("R_hat", "ESS") %in% colnames(est))) {
>       pars <- rownames(est)
>       if (is.null(pars) || !length(pars)) pars <- attr(d$estimates, "parameters")
>       rhat <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(est$R_hat))
>       ess  <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(est$ESS))
>       df <- data.frame(Unit = as.character(pars),
>                        R_hat = round(rhat, 4), ESS = round(ess, 0),
>                        Flag = flag_vec(rhat, ess), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>       return(list(kind = "parameter", df = df))
>     }
>   }
> 
>   # --- Model-level fallback ---
>   dg <- d$diagnostics
>   if (!is.null(dg)) {
>     dg <- as.data.frame(dg)
>     if (nrow(dg) > 0 && all(c("max_R_hat", "min_ESS") %in% colnames(dg))) {
>       unit <- if ("Model" %in% colnames(dg)) paste("Model", dg$Model) else paste("Model", seq_len(nrow(dg)))
>       rhat <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(dg$max_R_hat))
>       ess  <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(dg$min_ESS))
>       df <- data.frame(Unit = unit,
>                        R_hat = round(rhat, 4), ESS = round(ess, 0),
>                        Flag = flag_vec(rhat, ess), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>       return(list(kind = "model", df = df))
>     }
>   }
>   NULL
> }
> summary_row <- function(dl, label) {
>   if (is.null(dl) || is.null(dl$df) || nrow(dl$df) == 0) {
>     return(data.frame(Model = label, max_R_hat = NA_real_, min_ESS = NA_real_,
>                       Status = "unavailable", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
>   }
>   df <- dl$df
>   status <- if (any(df$Flag == "BAD")) "BAD" else if (any(df$Flag == "WARN")) "WARN" else "ok"
>   data.frame(
>     Model     = label,
>     max_R_hat = suppressWarnings(max(df$R_hat, na.rm = TRUE)),
>     min_ESS   = suppressWarnings(min(df$ESS,  na.rm = TRUE)),
>     Status    = status,
>     stringsAsFactors = FALSE
>   )
> }
> tex_label <- function(x) gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "-", x)
> print_diag_table <- function(dl, caption, label = NULL) {
>   if (is.null(dl) || is.null(dl$df) || nrow(dl$df) == 0) {
>     cat("\n*Diagnostics unavailable for this model.*\n\n")
>     return(invisible())
>   }
>   df       <- dl$df
>   unit_lab <- if (dl$kind == "model") "Ensemble model" else "Parameter"
>   k <- knitr::kable(
>     df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE,
>     align = c("l", "r", "r", "c"),
>     col.names = c(unit_lab, "R-hat", "ESS", "Flag"),
>     caption = caption,
>     label = if (!is.null(label)) tex_label(label) else NULL
>   )
>   k <- kableExtra::kable_styling(
>     k, latex_options = c("repeat_header", "hold_position", "striped"),
>     full_width = FALSE, font_size = 9
>   )
>   cat(k, "\n\n")
>   invisible()
> }
> print_gg_leaves <- function(obj) {
>   if (is.null(obj)) return(invisible())
>   if (inherits(obj, "ggplot")) {
>     print(obj)
>     cat("\n\n")
>     return(invisible())
>   }
>   if (is.list(obj)) {
>     for (i in seq_along(obj)) print_gg_leaves(obj[[i]])
>   }
>   invisible()
> }
> render_trace_plots <- function(fit, params = base_params) {
>   preds      <- fit$add_info[["predictors"]]
>   all_params <- unique(c(params, if (!is.null(preds)) preds))
> 
>   any_plotted <- FALSE
>   for (p in all_params) {
>     res <- NULL
>     # capture.output() swallows any stray text diagnostics() prints to stdout
>     # (e.g. "NULL"), which would otherwise leak into the asis output.
>     tryCatch(
>       utils::capture.output(
>         res <- RoBMA::diagnostics(fit, parameter = p, type = "trace", plot_type = "ggplot")
>       ),
>       error = function(e) NULL
>     )
>     if (is.null(res)) next
>     any_plotted <- TRUE
>     cat(sprintf("\n\n**Parameter: `%s`**\n\n", p))
>     print_gg_leaves(res)
>   }
>   if (!any_plotted) cat("\n*No trace plots available for this model.*\n\n")
>   invisible()
> }
> report_fit <- function(fit, label, heading_level = "##") {
>   cat(sprintf("\n\n%s %s\n\n", heading_level, nice_label(label)))
> 
>   dl <- diag_table(fit)
>   print_diag_table(dl, caption = paste0("R-hat and ESS --- ", nice_label(label)),
>                    label = paste0("diag-", label))
> 
>   summary_rows[[label]] <<- summary_row(dl, label)
> 
>   cat("\n\n**Trace plots**\n\n")
>   render_trace_plots(fit)
>   invisible()
> }

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
