Results

Literature search and study selection

The flow of the study selection process is presented in Figure 1. A systematic search yielded 6,041 potentially relevant articles, of which 367 remained after removing duplicates and screening titles and abstracts. Following the initial screening, 207 articles were retained after the full-text review. Based on the predefined eligibility criteria, 49 articles from 48 independent intervention studies published between 2010 and 2024 were included in the meta-analysis. The included studies comprised 181 effects across diverse cognitive outcomes. Details of the study characteristics are presented in Supplemental Materials (Table S1).

Participant details

The analyzed sample across all 48 studies was 2,605 participants, with a mean study sample size of 54.27 (SD = 57.26, range = 20-349). Although the average age across studies was 70.11 years, study mean ages spanned a wide range (SD = 8.42, range = 50-85). Excluding one study that did not report details about participants' age, 23 studies focused on older adults over 70 years of age, 13 studies on adults between 66 and 70 years, and 11 studies on adults between 50 and 65 years old. The average proportion of male participants across studies was 38.69%.

Of the 48 studies, 15 recruited non-clinical samples aged 50 and above (n = 861) (Adcock et al., 2020; Carrasco et al., 2020; Gouveia et al., 2021; Guimarães, A. V. et al., 2018; D. R. Kim et al., 2021; T. Kim & Xiong, 2022; Olyaei et al., 2022; Ordnung et al., 2017; J. Park & Yim, 2016; Phirom et al., 2020; Schättin et al., 2016; Sturnieks et al., 2024; Wais et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Zak et al., 2022). The remaining studies focused on adults over 50 with clinical conditions, grouped as follows: cardiovascular conditions (e.g., stroke, metabolic syndrome, hypertension; k = 9; n = 411) (Cai et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; Hou et al., 2023; B. R. Kim et al., 2011; M. Park & Ha, 2023; Rozental-Iluz et al., 2016; Şimşek & Çekok, 2016; Unibaso-Markaida et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019), reduced mobility (e.g., wheelchair use, post-fall rehabilitation; k = 5; n = 442) (W. L. S. Chan et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2012; Hassett et al., 2020; Y. Y. Liao et al., 2021; Maggio et al., 2022), neurocognitive or psychiatric conditions (e.g., mild cognitive impairment, ADRD, schizophrenia; k = 13; n = 656) (Amjad et al., 2019; C. L. Chan et al., 2010; De Luca et al., 2023; Hsieh et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2014; Karssemeijer et al., 2019; Y.-Y. Liao et al., 2019; Swinnen et al., 2021; Thapa et al., 2020; van Santen et al., 2020; Wiloth et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2022), and Parkinson's disease (k = 6; n = 235) (Droby et al., 2020; Hajebrahimi et al., 2022; Nuic et al., 2024; Pompeu et al., 2012; Song et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2014).

Geographically, the 48 studies were conducted across five regions: Asia (k = 26), Europe (k = 15), Oceania (k = 3), North America (k = 2), and South America (k = 2).

Intervention characteristics

Exergaming interventions varied widely in duration, frequency, and overall length. Session durations ranged from 15 to 100 minutes (M = 45.52, SD = 20.50): fewer than 30 minutes (k = 8), 30-45 minutes (k = 20), and more than 45 minutes (k = 20). Training frequency ranged from 1 to ), and 5 days/week (k = 4).

Intervention durations spanned 3 to 26 weeks (M = 10.45, SD = 6.01).

Regarding exergaming platforms, 30 studies employed screen-based gaming consoles, while 18 studies used VR-based systems. Among the screen-based interventions, the Nintendo Wii or Wii U (k = 10) and Microsoft Xbox Kinect (k = 10) were the most frequently used, followed by dance pad or dance platform systems (k = 5). Of the VR-based systems, 5 studies used fully immersive headsets, while the remaining 13 utilized room-scale VR installations. Most studies (k = 30) used commercially available exergames. The remaining 18 studies used researcherdeveloped exergames tailored to specific intervention goals.

Most studies (k = 41) did not require an internet connection to play. Exergames were also coded for narrative integration as a motivational design feature (Lu, 2015). Only one game, Nintendo Ring Fit Adventure, included some narrative components.

In terms of setting, 25 studies were conducted in field environments, including 13 in hospitals, 6 in group living facilities, 3 in home environments, and 3 in physical therapy practices.

Further, 9 studies were conducted in laboratory settings, and 3 studies did not specify a setting.

The remaining 11 studies were conducted across multiple or alternative settings.

Most studies compared exergaming against an alternative treatment control condition (k = 28). Note that all these studies included populations with clinical conditions. Additionally, a smaller proportion of studies used active control groups (k = 9) or only a passive control (k = 9).

The remaining two studies included two control groups: an alternative treatment and a passive control group (Hou et al., 2023), and an active and a passive control group (Sturnieks et al., 2024).

Risk of bias

The distribution of risk-of-bias scores is presented in Figure 2. Overall, the mean risk-ofbias score was 0.44 (SD = 0.40; range: -0.43 to 1.00). The most common high-risk factor was the lack of blinding of participants and personnel, observed in 58% of studies. Additionally, 33% of studies demonstrated risk of bias due to lack of blinding in outcome assessment, and approximately 27% showed risk of bias due to inadequate allocation concealment. In contrast, the most frequently observed indicators of a low risk of bias were complete reporting of outcome data (98%), use of random assignment (83%), avoidance of selective reporting (75%), and efforts to minimize other sources of bias (75%).

Main outcomes

A total of 181 effect sizes were extracted, each representing a cognitive measure. These outcomes were initially categorized into 15 cognitive domains and subsequently consolidated into 11 cognitive domains as explained above (see Methods). Because some studies contributed with multiple outcomes, the total sample size in each domain exceeds the total sample size due to within-study multiplicity. The 11 cognitive domains included: global cognition (k = 29; n = 1,584), processing speed (k = 23; n = 1,163), cognitive flexibility (k = 22; n = 1,544), attentional control (k = 16; n = 916), working memory (k = 14; n = 897), short-term memory (k = 8; n = 569), longterm memory (k = 7; n = 261), visuospatial processing (k = 6; n = 249), motor control (k = 3; n = 154), language (k = 4; n = 423), and episodic memory (k = 2; n = 154). We use the term "global cognition" to refer to screening measures for older adults' global cognitive functioning, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) (Nasreddine et al., 2005) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) (Folstein et al., 1983). A detailed list of examples of tasks used to assess each cognitive outcome domain is available in Supplemental Materials (Table S2).

Overall effect on cognition

First, we evaluated the overall impact of exergames on cognition using a Bayesian multilevel meta-analytic model. This model pooled 181 effect sizes across all cognitive domains, enabling estimation of a study-level average effect while accounting for intra-study dependency due to multiple cognitive outcomes reported within the same study. The meta-analysis revealed that the standardized mean difference (SMD) was 0.31 (BF10 > 1000) suggesting a small positive effect of exergames across cognitive outcomes (K = 48). The total heterogeneity was 0.25 (95% CrI = [0.17, 0.34]; BF10 > 1000), indicating decisive evidence for moderate variability in effect sizes across studies.

To evaluate the potential impact of publication bias on the overall effect across cognitive outcomes, we examined a funnel plot and conducted the Egger's regression test. Figure 3 shows the funnel plot of observed effect sizes against their standard errors, where visual inspection suggests funnel-plot asymmetry. Specifically, there is a skew toward studies reporting positive effects of exergames on cognition. Individual effect sizes and their 95% confidence intervals are shown in the forest plot in the Supplemental Materials (forest_plot_all_outcomes.pdf). Egger's regression analysis did not provide strong support for the visual impression of publication bias (estimate = 0.14; 95% CrI = [-0.24, 0.51]; BF10 = 1.25). The estimated effect after accounting for small-study effects in the Egger regression was SMD = 0.27 (95% CrI = [0.13, 0.42]; BF10 = 68.98). On the other hand, after accounting for publication bias using the multilevel RoBMA framework, the estimated SMD was 0.13 (BF10 = 1.05), and the publication bias inclusion factor provided anecdotal evidence for publication bias (BF10 = 2.39) in line with Egger's regression test.

Multilevel RoBMA yielded a smaller adjusted estimate than the Egger regression, and the evidence for an overall effect after adjusting for publication bias was inconclusive. RoBMA Model. Notes: Each data point represents one observed effect size (i.e., 181 effect sizes from 48 independent studies). The white background represents the 95% region of the sampling distribution of observed effect sizes implied by the model-averaged multilevel RoBMA fit, incorporating The Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis by cognitive domain, revealed small effects of 593 exergaming across the five cognitive outcomes examined prior to accounting for publication bias (Table 1, NoBMA). For global cognition, a small effect (SMD = 0.37, BF10 > 1000) was observed accompanied by substantial between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.39; 95% CrI = [0.25, 0.56]; BF10 > 1000). A small effect was found for processing speed (SMD = 0.28, BF10 = 52.25) with moderate between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.28; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.47]; BF10 = 26.32). For cognitive flexibility, a small effect was also observed (SMD = 0.21, BF10 = 13.04) with moderate heterogeneity (τ = 0.23; 95% CrI = [0, 0.42]; BF10 = 9.04). A small effect was detected for attentional control (SMD = 0.23, BF10 = 356.91) with very low heterogeneity (τ = 0.01; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.16]; BF10 = 0.15). Finally, working memory showed a small effect (SMD = 0.21, BF10 = 12.62) with low heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.38]; BF10 = 0.55).

After accounting for publication bias (multilevel RoBMA), there was anecdotal evidence for a small positive effect of exergaming on global cognition, and substantial uncertainty around the magnitude of the effect (SMD = 0.23, 95% CrI = [0.00, 0.49]; BF10 = 2.47). There was anecdotal evidence for effects on processing speed (SMD = 0.14, BF10 = 1.35). There was anecdotal evidence favoring the null hypothesis for cognitive flexibility (SMD = 0.08, BF10 = 0.63). There was anecdotal evidence for a positive effect on attentional control (SMD = 0.11, BF10 = 1.32). For working memory, the data favored the null hypothesis after accounting for publication bias (SMD = 0.04, BF10 = 0.33). Importantly, the evidence for publication bias varied across cognitive domains. There was anecdotal evidence favoring publication bias models for global cognition (BF10 bias = 1.18), processing speed (BF10 bias = 1.61), attentional control (BF10 bias = 1.68) and cognitive flexibility (BF10 bias = 2.49), with the strongest evidence for publication bias observed for working memory (BF10 bias = 10.08). There was no evidence that mean age or population condition moderated the effect of exergaming on cognition, with inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models. Thus, the data favored models excluding these participant-level characteristics as moderators.

Intervention-design and methodological factors

Effects of intervention dosage.

There was little evidence that intervention dosage moderated the effects of exergaming on cognition. Session duration and session frequency showed inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models, favoring models excluding these factors. Intervention duration yielded only anecdotal evidence for inclusion before and after accounting for model uncertainty and publication bias (NoBMA BF10 = 2.62; RoBMA BF10 = 1.25), with slightly smaller estimates for interventions with longer duration.

Effects of exergame modality and product type.

There was no evidence that exergame modality (VR-based vs. screen-based exergames) moderated intervention effects, with inclusion Bayes factors below 1 in both NoBMA and RoBMA models. Similarly, product type (commercially available vs. researcher-developed exergames) showed no evidence for moderation (NoBMA BF10 = 0.44; RoBMA BF10 = 0.42).

Effects of methodological characteristics.

Among the methodological factors examined, the evidence did not support the inclusion of control type as moderating factor (NoBMA BF10 = 0.18; RoBMA BF10 = 0.16).

Blinding showed no evidence for moderator inclusion, indicating limited evidence that intervention effects differed according to blinding status (NoBMA BF10 = 0.30; RoBMA BF10 = 0.25). Further, risk of bias showed no evidence for moderator inclusion in either modeling approach (NoBMA BF10 = 0.29; RoBMA BF10 = 0.29).

Overall, these findings suggest that, after accounting for heterogeneity, model uncertainty, and publication bias, individual-level and methodological factors did not show evidence supporting their role as moderators. These exploratory findings should be confirmed in future meta-analyses with a larger evidence base, which would increase statistical power to detect moderator effects.

Sensitivity analysis

We evaluated the sensitivity of the findings to alternative prior specifications. For the overall effect and the cognitive domains, we tested alternative effect priors [N(0, 0.25), N(0.30, 0.30), and N(0, 1)] relative to the primary N(0.30, 0.15) prior, as well as the RoBMA default prior for heterogeneity. For the meta-regression, we retained the primary prior for the overall effect and tested a zero-centered prior [N(0, 0.15)] for moderator effects relative to the primary N(0.05, 0.15) specification. After adjusting for publication bias, the evidence for an overall effect remained inconclusive under the N(0, 0.25) and N(0.30, 0.30) priors (BF₁₀ = 0.74 and 0.70 respectively) and under the default heterogeneity prior (BF₁₀ = 1.02), and it favored the null hypothesis under the wider N(0, 1) default RoBMA prior (BF₁₀ = 0.29). No moderator showed evidence for inclusion under the alternative moderator prior (RoBMA BF₁₀ ≤ 1.67).

We also examined the sensitivity of the overall findings to alternative assumed pre-post correlations (r = 0.20 and 0.80, relative to r = 0.50 in the primary analysis). As expected, the assumed correlation affected effect-size magnitude and evidence strength (RoBMA: SMD = 0.17, BF₁₀ = 2.77 and SMD = 0.00, BF₁₀ = 0.10, respectively), but the evidence did not support a robust overall effect under either assumption.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we repeated the analyses after excluding studies that did not use fully randomized allocation procedures (k = 41; 167 effect sizes). The overall effect was slightly attenuated (NoBMA: SMD = 0.28; BF10 > 1000; RoBMA: SMD = 0.11; BF10 = 0.93), the evidence for publication bias remained anecdotal (BF₁₀ = 2.30), and no cognitive domain showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect. The evidence for an overall effect also remained inconclusive when excluding effect sizes whose standard deviations were derived from standard errors, interquartile ranges or ranges (BF10 = 0.95) and when excluding studies at high risk of bias in random sequence generation, allocation concealment or outcome-assessor blinding (BF₁₀ = 0.85, 1.23 and 0.83, respectively), and it ranged from BF₁₀ = 0.46 to 3.43 when each study was left out (leave-one-out analysis).

To address the dependence between sampling errors of outcomes measured in the same participants, we also aggregated effect sizes within studies assuming within-study correlations of r = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 (Borenstein et al., 2009). The evidence for an overall effect remained inconclusive (RoBMA BF₁₀ = 2.50, 1.77 and 1.64, respectively), and only processing speed showed moderate evidence for an effect in two of these aggregated models (BF₁₀ = 3.59, BF₁₀ = 3.36; r = 0.30, 0.50 and 0.70 respectively). Convergence was considered as satisfactory in the models fitted for the main analysis. The leave-one-study-out refits were run with lighter MCMC settings and were not included in the convergence diagnostics. In total, the sensitivity analyses comprised 160 additional models (including 48 leave-one-study-out refits). A full report of the sensitivity analysis conducted, and the convergence diagnostics of the models tested, can be found in Supplemental Materials (Sensitivity_Outputs_Report.html).

Discussion

This meta-analysis reassessed the magnitude, uncertainty, and robustness of the evidence on the cognitive effects of exergames in adults aged 50 and above published up to May 31, 2024.

To do it, we employed Bayesian meta-analytic techniques which allow to quantify the uncertainty and robustness of the effects (Moran & Linden, 2024; Röver et al., 2021). Accordingly, we investigated the impact on cognitive outcomes of exergaming interventions among adults aged 50 and above, guided by three primary questions: (i) Do exergame interventions improve cognition in this population? (ii) Are the effects moderated by individual factors? and (iii) Are the effects moderated by methodological factors related to the intervention? This study extends previous work by offering a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous synthesis of exergames' cognitive effects in middle-aged and older adults. Several aspects of the present findings warrant further discussion, particularly regarding methodological limitations observed in prior research and the implications for future implementations of exergames as cognitive interventions for middle-aged and older adults.

Do exergame interventions improve cognitive outcomes?

Do exergame interventions improve cognitive outcomes?

Overall effect

Without adjustment for publication bias our findings support a small positive effect of exergames on cognition. However, after accounting for publication bias, heterogeneity, and model uncertainty, the estimated effect was attenuated and the evidence was inconclusive. The evidence for publication bias was anecdotal though and therefore, the adjusted estimate should be understood as an average across models with and without publication bias weighted by their posterior probabilities. This result is consistent with previous findings where effects became largely attenuated after accounting for publication bias (Sala et al., 2021). In their commentary on Stanmore et al. (2017), Sala et al. (2021) concluded that the apparent benefits of exergames become negligible after bias correction, based primarily on trim-and-fill and PET-PEESE adjustments.

RoBMA treats publication bias as a model uncertainty problem by estimating an ensemble of models that vary in whether publication bias, heterogeneity, and non-zero effects are present, relying on model-averaging inferences. This framework reduces dependence on any single correction method chosen and explicitly propagates the uncertainty about the bias process into the pooled estimate (Maier et al., 2023).

Effects by cognitive outcome

The analyses by cognitive domain mirrored the overall effect. That is, the positive estimates across all five domains were attenuated once publication bias was taken into account, leaving no cognitive domain with more than anecdotal evidence for an effect. The evidence was anecdotal for global cognition which here referred to cognition screening measures such as the MoCA (Nasreddine et al., 2005) or the MMSE (Folstein et al., 1983), processing speed and attentional control. The evidence was inconclusive for cognitive flexibility and favored the null hypothesis for working memory, the domain with the strongest evidence of publication bias. From a game design perspective, the anecdotal evidence for domain-specific effects on cognition might still be informative. The small and anecdotal effects observed may reflect the real-time cognitive and motor-control demands inherent in exergame play, where players must continuously select taskrelevant information, manage interference, and adjust quickly their actions in response to rapid changing in-game demands (Maggio et al., 2025; Olyaei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Wollesen et al., 2020). We acknowledge that although this finding suggests a degree of domain specificity, caution is warranted for several reasons. Numerical differences in the strength of evidence across domains do not establish that exergames affect some domains more than others, as these differences were not directly tested. Moreover, core EFs, such as attentional control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory, are highly interrelated, depend on overlapping brain networks, and are often measured with tasks that are not process-pure (Friedman & Miyake, 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Niendam et al., 2012). As such, isolating domain-specific effects is inherently difficult. Furthermore, task variability across studies likely contributes to the high heterogeneity observed in these outcomes (see Supplemental Materials, Table S2). Thus, whether specific design features, such as the real-time attentional and motor-control demands of exergame play or adaptive difficulty, can produce domain-specific benefits remains an hypothesis for future trials (Grosprêtre et al., 2023; Wollesen et al., 2020).

Do individual factors moderate exergame intervention effectiveness?

Do individual factors moderate exergame intervention effectiveness?

Effects as a function of age and population characteristics

One of the main goals of the present study was to examine whether the efficacy of exergaming interventions varies as a function of participants' age and population characteristics, given the substantial heterogeneity observed across the literature.

Exergaming interventions have been investigated in adults aged 50 and above across both non-clinical and clinical samples, including people with mild cognitive impairment and ADRD, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and limited mobility. Despite the diverse sample included in the present work, the metaregression provided evidence against moderation of the overall effect by age or population clinical condition in line with Manser et al. (2024). These results suggest that, with the current evidence, the effects of exergames on cognition do not seem to differ substantially across age groups or between clinical and non-clinical populations. However, given the limited number of studies per subgroup and the substantial heterogeneity within them, these analyses should be considered exploratory and therefore, differences of smaller magnitude cannot be ruled out.

Do methodological and intervention design factors moderate the impact of exergames on cognition?

Do methodological and intervention design factors moderate the impact of exergames on cognition?

Effects of intervention dosage

Our results revealed no conclusive evidence for a dose-response relationship between exergaming and cognitive improvement in adults aged 50 and above. These results are consistent with Manser et al. (2024), who found limited evidence for dose-response effects of exergame interventions and their impact on cognitive functioning.

Several factors may explain the lack of moderating effects concerning dose-response intervention characteristics. The moderators such as "session duration", "session frequency", and "total intervention duration" were characterized by imbalanced distributions across levels, which, along with high heterogeneity, likely undermined the statistical power and the likelihood of observing a moderation effect (Hempel et al., 2013). Further, intervention duration showed a small negative association with effect size, with only anecdotal evidence for its inclusion, raising the possibility that cognitive benefits may not increase with longer training. Whether cognitive benefits plateau or diminish with extended training due to fatigue, reduced engagement, or compliance issues should be directly examined in future studies. Importantly, none of the 48 included studies explicitly tested dose-response hypotheses. Thus, this meta-analysis highlights the critical need for targeted randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that systematically manipulate intervention dose to determine optimal configuration for supporting cognitive health in aging adults, in line with prior recommendations (Manser et al., 2024; Torre & Temprado, 2022).

Effects of exergame modality and product type

There was no evidence that exergame modality (VR-based vs. screen-based) or product type (researcher-developed vs. commercially available) moderated the effects of exergames on cognition. In both cases, the evidence was inconclusive after accounting for publication bias. It likely reflects the imbalanced distribution of exergame types used, with most studies using commercial, screen-based exergames, as well as the residual heterogeneity across studies. Since exergame modality only contrasted screen-based with VR-based systems, finer-grained distinctions such as between platform generations or specific design features (e.g., immersion, adaptive difficulty), could not be tested and remain open questions. Researcher-developed exergames allow greater targeting of specific cognitive processes through tailored design (Seitz et al., 2023), and emerging interventions, such as Brain-IT, which combines multidomain exergaming with heart-rate variability biofeedback (Manser & de Bruin, 2024), illustrate this potential. Yet, such benefits were not established by the present analyses. By contrast, commercial titles are typically optimized primarily for entertainment and retention purposes rather than for a particular cognitive outcome (Sailer et al., 2017), which has also been suggested to be critical for improving their clinical effectiveness (Torre & Temprado, 2022). Future trials should directly compare exergame modalities and design features to determine how they influence cognitive outcomes.

Limitations

This meta-analysis is not exempt from limitations. Each article was extracted by a welltrained primary coder, and then independently verified against the source by two additional coders with continuous inter-rater reliability monitoring, as well as full-group consensus resolution. This single-extraction-with-independent-verification model is not equivalent to fully independent, blinded duplicate extraction, which remains the gold standard in systematic reviews (Higgins, J. P. T. et al., 2019). Because the additional coders verified the primary coders' extraction rather than extracting the data independently, some anchoring to the initial coding cannot be excluded.

Nevertheless, the use of standardized extraction forms, extensive coder training, independent

Running Head: Impact of Exergames on Cognition in Midlife and Older Age

This manuscript is a preprint verification against the source, continuous monitoring of inter-rater reliability, and consensus resolution of discrepancies provided multiple safeguards to minimize extraction errors (Büchter et al., 2020; Garritty et al., 2021). Another limitation of this meta-analysis is that only published studies in English were included, in accordance with the pre-registered PROSPERO protocol (ID: CRD42020204191). While this approach ensured methodological consistency and transparency, it may have excluded relevant unpublished or non-English studies. Future reviews could expand the search to include grey literature and studies published in other languages to provide a more comprehensive synthesis of global evidence. The inclusion of studies where exergaming comprised >50% of the intervention is another limitation. While this threshold ensured that exergaming was the dominant component and reflected real-world practice, the choice may introduce confounds, as some cognitive benefits could also be attributed to non-exergame components. As such, efficacy claims specific to exergaming should be interpreted cautiously, and this approach may reduce comparability with prior reviews that applied stricter inclusion criteria.

Moreover, seven of the included studies used pseudo-randomized rather than fully randomized allocation procedures. Although these studies met the predefined eligibility criteria for controlled intervention designs, the absence of full randomization may increase susceptibility to selection bias and limit the strength of causal inference from this work. Nevertheless, sensitivity analyses restricted to fully randomized studies largely preserved the pattern of findings, although effect estimates and Bayesian evidence were generally attenuated. A further statistical limitation is that although the multilevel models accounted for the clustering of effect sizes within studies, they did not directly model the sampling covariance among effect sizes derived from the same participants.

However, aggregating effect sizes within studies under plausible within-study correlations led to similar conclusions, except for processing speed which showed moderate evidence for an effect only in the aggregated models. Additionally, this meta-analysis was limited in its ability to examine differential effects on all cognitive outcomes due to the large variability of measures across studies. Further, although this meta-analysis included a relatively large number of studies, the evidence base remained insufficient to examine interactions among moderators. Another limitation is that the coverage of studies published before 2016 depends on the reviews identified

Future Directions

Several directions for future research emerge from our findings and from the methodological limitations of the existing literature.

1. The current evidence is based mostly on studies with small samples and limited statistical power. While typical in emerging research areas, such limitations restrict the generalizability of meta-analytic findings and hinder the exploration of potential moderators. Thus, large-scale, wellpowered RCTs preregistered trials are needed to clarify for whom, and under which conditions, exergaming might yield cognitive benefits (Jaeggi et al., 2014; Parong et al., 2022).

2. We observed considerable variability in how EFs were assessed and operationalized. To enhance comparability across studies, future research would benefit from (i) the adoption of standardized cognitive assessment batteries, such as the National Institute of Health (NIH) toolbox for Neurological and Behavioral Function Cognition Battery (NIH Toolbox CB) (Gershon et al., 2013), as well as from (ii) operationalizing EFs through joint measures of speed-accuracy (for a review see : Liesefeld & Janczyk, 2019; Yangüez et al., 2024) or parameters derived from diffusion models (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008). The latter is particularly relevant in research including older adults, who tend to prioritize accuracy over speed (Starns & Ratcliff, 2012), so changes in either measure alone may reflect shifts in response strategy rather than genuine improvements in cognitive function.

3. Blinding remains a key methodological issue in the literature, not only in exergame interventions but in gamified cognitive and physical interventions more broadly (Kletzel et al., 2021; Pacheco et al., 2020). Future studies should aim for blinded outcome assessment when feasible, for instance, blinding evaluators to participants' group assignments or leveraging selfadministered digital platforms to minimize bias (Öhman et al., 2021). 6. Another plausible mechanism is improvement in cardiovascular fitness which has been linked to cognitive enhancement and neuroplasticity in prior research (Kramer & Colcombe, 2018; Voss et al., 2016). During the literature review conducted, however, only seven of the 48 studies included measured cardiovascular fitness as one of their outcomes. While we acknowledge that it is not feasible to include in every intervention a gold-standard measure of cardiovascular fitness (e.g., maximal oxygen uptake testing). There are, however, validated alternatives such as the 1mile timed walk or computational estimates of cardiovascular fitness based on age, sex, body mass index, resting heart rate, and self-reported physical activity level (Jurca et al., 2005; McAuley et al., 2011).

7. Interventions varied widely in their design and implementation. For example, among screen-based exergame interventions, some used dance platform systems, while others employed motion-based systems such as the Nintendo Wii or Microsoft Xbox Kinect. These systems differ in gameplay mechanics, user interaction styles, and likely engage different levels of physical and cognitive stimulation (Busser et al., 2024), which might impact their effect on EFs, as prior metaanalytic evidence suggests (Manser et al., 2024). We recommend that future exergame trials characterize their interventions using an established design or gamification taxonomy (e.g., feedback, progression, and social mechanics), thereby allowing future meta-analyses to test these features as moderators. Standardized reporting of this kind would also advance the field by identifying which design characteristics are responsible for cognitive gains and in which populations.

8. Personalization and user-centered designs also warrant attention. Tailoring exergames to the physical and cognitive needs of older users may increase both accessibility and efficacy (Torre & Temprado, 2022). Promising recent work has shown cognitive improvements among older adults with mild neurocognitive disorders using heart-rate biofeedback (Manser & de Bruin, 2024). Further, closed-loop, adaptive technologies could dynamically adjust cognitive and physical difficulty, providing an optimal challenge tailored to individual capacity (Anguera et al., 2022).

9. The field would also benefit from longitudinal follow-up studies to assess the degree to which gains are maintained over time. Only eight of the 48 studies in this review included followup assessments, leaving open questions about the persistence of cognitive gains and whether periodic "booster" sessions are necessary to maintain benefits. Understanding the longevity and transferability of cognitive benefits from exergames would be essential for evaluating the longterm utility of exergames in cognitive aging and their impact, if any, on real-life outcomes.

10. Finally, the field may also benefit from moving toward open and updateable evidence syntheses that can evolve alongside the rapidly growing literature. To facilitate this, the complete https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22756576 analytical framework to evolve as methodological standards develop.

Conclusions

The findings of the present meta-analysis indicate that, after accounting for publication bias, the evidence about the effects of exergames on cognition was inconclusive. This pattern was consistent across sensitivity analyses, and no cognitive domain showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect. Likewise, there was no evidence that the effects differed by population or intervention characteristics. These findings do not show that exergames are ineffective, but that the current evidence base does not allow to establish firm conclusions about their impact on cognition. Since the apparent benefit of exergames largely depended on whether publication bias was taken into account, as the field continues to evolve, there is a pressing need for larger and well-powered preregistered trials. Additionally, the use of standardized cognitive assessments, blinded outcome evaluation, adequately matched controls, and follow-up assessments, as well as mechanistic research will be essential to determine whether exergames can provide reliable and clinically meaningful cognitive benefits for middle-aged and older adults.

Finally, the rapid growth of exergaming research has been accompanied by increasing heterogeneity in intervention characteristics, study designs, cognitive outcome measures, and participant populations, which challenges the reproducibility and comparability of evidence syntheses. Future systematic reviews and meta-analyses would therefore benefit from greater methodological standardization, including independent duplicate study selection and data extraction, transparent and reproducible classification of cognitive outcome domains, and the use of risk-of-bias tools matched to study design, such as RoB 2 for randomized controlled trials and ROBINS-I for non-randomized intervention studies (J. A.Sterne et al., 2016; J. A. C. Sterne et al., 2019).

4.

Active control conditions should match exergames in engagement and expectation, ideally tested alongside passive control groups. In the present literature, the type of group control was largely confounded with population characteristics, as alternative-treatment controls were used almost exclusively in clinical samples. More RCTs conducted on clinical populations including both passive and alternative-treatment controls would help disentangle these factors.5. Mechanistic research on exercise dose and intensity is also needed. Future work should investigate the optimal dose of exergame interventions(Colcombe & Kramer, 2003), balancing session duration, frequency, and total training volume with considerations of fatigue and sustained motivation. The role of type of exercise and exercise intensity on cognition deserves further attention. WhileManser et al. (2024) reported stronger effects with moderate-intensity exergaming, intensity data were only available for fewer than 60% of the studies (k = 30), underscoring the need for experimental manipulation and reporting of low intensity (e.g., tai chi, yoga) vs. high intensity (e.g., biking) interventions.
